Nearly every meaning of "high" as an adjective comes from one simple idea — being above a reference point. That reference point could be the ground, a normal level, an average, a rank, or a sober state of mind. Once you grasp that central thread, all the different meanings will feel connected and logical.
1. Physically Elevated — Far from the Ground

The most basic meaning: something is located far above the ground or far above its base.

  • "The bird built its nest in a high branch."
  • "The high shelves are hard to reach."
  • "Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth."
  • "The plane was flying at a high altitude."

High vs. Tall — an important distinction:

Many learners confuse these two words. Here is the difference:

  • Tall describes how much something extends from its base to its top — its physical size. You use it when you're talking about the size of the object itself. "A tall man." "A tall tree." "A tall building."
  • High describes how far something is from the ground — its position or location. "A high shelf." "A high branch." "A high cliff." "A high window."

A useful test: if you're measuring the object's own size, use tall. If you're describing where something is, or how far above the ground it is, use high.

Both words can describe buildings: "a tall building" (focusing on its size) and "a high building" (focusing on it being elevated above the ground) are both natural. But you would not say "a high man" to mean a tall person — that would sound wrong. And "a high cliff" is more natural than "a tall cliff."

Also note: in geography, "high" often refers to elevation above sea level. "The city sits at a high altitude" means it is far above sea level.
2. Above a Normal or Average Level — Measurable Things

Whenever something can be measured — temperature, price, speed, blood pressure, risk — "high" means the measurement is significantly above normal or average.

  • High temperature: much warmer than normal. "She has a high fever." / "High temperatures are forecast this week."
  • High price: something costs a lot of money. "Rent in this city is very high."
  • High speed: moving very fast. "The car traveled at high speed."
  • High blood pressure: the force of blood pushing through your vessels is greater than it should be.
  • High risk: a great probability that something bad will happen.
  • High quality: an excellent standard.
  • High score: you performed exceptionally well.
  • High unemployment: a large percentage of people out of work.

The logic is always the same: you imagine a scale, and "high" simply means the value is toward the top of that scale. The opposite is always low.
3. Great in Degree or Intensity — Non-Measurable Things

Even when something cannot be put on a numerical scale, "high" expresses that something is strong, intense, or extreme in degree.

  • High hopes: very strong desires or expectations for a good outcome. "She had high hopes for her son's career."
  • High praise: very enthusiastic, positive praise. "The film received high praise from critics."
  • High expectations: expecting a great deal from someone or something.
  • High anxiety: feeling very anxious.
  • High drama: a situation that is intensely tense, emotional, or exciting.
  • High priority: something that demands attention more urgently than other things.
  • High alert: a state of strong readiness or heightened watchfulness, usually for danger.
  • High pressure: used figuratively to mean stressful, demanding conditions. "A high-pressure job."
4. Senior in Rank, Status, or Importance

"High" describes people, positions, or institutions that are above others in a hierarchy — whether that's a government, a legal system, the military, or society.

  • High official: a senior government or organizational official.
  • High court: a superior or supreme court of law. (In many countries, "the High Court" is the proper name of a powerful court.)
  • High command: the most senior military leaders.
  • High society: the wealthy and socially prominent upper class.
  • High office: an important, senior position of power.
  • High priest: the most senior priest; also used figuratively for someone who is the leading authority in a field. "He is considered the high priest of modern architecture."
  • High-ranking: holding a senior position. "A high-ranking official."

The metaphor is transparent: in any hierarchy, important people are "above" others — they are at the top, or at a high position.
5. Advanced, Complex, or Sophisticated

"High" indicates something is at a more advanced, refined, or intellectually sophisticated level than what is ordinary or basic.

  • Higher education: university-level education, which comes after basic schooling.
  • High culture: art, literature, classical music, and other pursuits considered refined and intellectual — as opposed to popular or mass entertainment.
  • High art: serious, complex art, not commercial or decorative work.
  • Higher mathematics: advanced mathematics beyond basic arithmetic — calculus, abstract algebra, etc.
  • High technology (also high-tech): the most advanced, cutting-edge technology.
  • High fashion: the most exclusive and creative world of clothing design.
  • High-minded: having strong, noble, or idealistic principles. "She was a high-minded reformer."
6. Having a Positive or Favorable Opinion

"High" expresses that your opinion or regard for someone or something is at a very favorable, positive level.

  • "I have a high opinion of her work." (= I think her work is excellent)
  • "He holds her in high regard." (= He respects and admires her greatly)
  • "She is highly regarded in her field." (= People think very well of her)
  • "She has a high opinion of herself." (= She thinks very well of herself — this can imply arrogance depending on context)

Think of it this way: on a scale from very negative to very positive, your opinion is at the "high" end.
7. Sound: High in Pitch

A sound is "high" when it vibrates quickly, producing a tone that is sharp, piercing, or shrill — as opposed to a deep, low sound.

  • "She has a very high voice." (a voice with a high pitch, like a soprano singer)
  • "That note is too high for me to reach."
  • "A high-pitched whistle."
  • "A high-pitched scream."

On a piano, the keys on the right side produce high notes; keys on the left produce low notes. The sounds of birds, flutes, or squeaking hinges are high. The sounds of drums, thunder, or a bass guitar are low.
8. At the Peak or Fullest Point in Time

"High" can describe the moment or period when something is at its fullest, most intense, or most complete stage.

  • High noon: exactly midday (12:00 PM), when the sun is at its highest point in the sky. This phrase also commonly means a moment of ultimate confrontation or decisive crisis, especially from the imagery of Western films.
  • High tide: the point in the ocean's daily cycle when the water level on the shore is at its highest. The opposite is "low tide."
  • High summer: the peak of summer — the hottest, brightest, most intense part of the season.
  • High season: the busiest and most popular time of year for tourism, travel, or a particular business.
  • High point: the best, most important, or most impressive moment of a period or event. "The concert was the high point of the festival."
  • It is high time: a fixed phrase meaning something should have been done already — it is well overdue. "It is high time you apologized." (= You should have apologized long ago; there is no more excuse for delay.)
9. Intoxicated — Under the Influence of a Substance

In informal but very widely used everyday speech, "high" describes the mental and physical state of feeling intoxicated, euphoric, or altered because of drugs (or sometimes alcohol).

  • "He was high on marijuana."
  • "She looked high — her eyes were glazed and she was speaking slowly."
  • "Some people get high to escape their stress."

The connection to the core idea is poetic: intoxication gives a person the feeling of being mentally "lifted" above their normal state of consciousness — a sense of elevation.
10. High and Mighty — Arrogant, Self-Important

The fixed phrase "high and mighty" describes someone who behaves as though they are superior to everyone else — arrogant, condescending, and dismissive.

  • "Don't get so high and mighty with me just because you got a promotion."
  • "He acts all high and mighty, but he started at the bottom like everyone else."
11. In High Spirits — Joyful, Lively, and Energetic

The fixed phrase "in high spirits" means feeling very happy, cheerful, lively, and full of energy. It is always positive.

  • "The team was in high spirits after winning the match."
  • "The children were in high spirits on the last day of school."
  • "Despite the setback, she remained in high spirits."
12. Strong-Smelling (of Food) — Old-Fashioned / Formal

In older English and formal culinary writing, especially when describing aged game meat (like pheasant or venison), "high" describes food that has been kept long enough to start decomposing slightly, giving it a strong, pungent smell. Some traditional cooks considered this desirable for flavor.

  • "The pheasant smells high — it has been hanging for a week."
  • "The cheese is quite high — that's how it's supposed to be."

This usage is rare in ordinary modern conversation but you may encounter it in older literature or formal food writing.
How "High" Behaves Grammatically

"High" works naturally in both positions:

Before a noun:
"A high mountain." / "A high price." / "High hopes." / "A high note."

After a verb:
"The mountain is very high." / "The price was too high." / "Her spirits were high."

It follows regular comparison:

  • Higher (comparative): "This floor is higher than the last." / "The new model comes at a higher price."
  • Highest (superlative): "That is the highest point in the country." / "She achieved the highest score in the class."
Important Fixed Phrases and Collocations

These are the most important word combinations you will encounter. Knowing these will help you understand and use "high" naturally.

High + noun (some of the most common):
high price, high cost, high temperature, high quality, high risk, high speed, high tide, high school, high court, high society, high noon, high street (British English: the main shopping street in a town), high time, high spirits, high priority, high alert, high season, high point, high voltage, high altitude, high heels, high hopes, high profile, high standard

Compound adjectives (high + another word, hyphenated):
high-quality, high-risk, high-tech, high-powered (very energetic or capable), high-profile (attracting a lot of public attention), high-end (expensive and of superior quality), high-pitched, high-minded (having noble principles)

Verbs and phrases used with high:

  • run high: emotions or tensions run high = they are very intense and difficult to control. "Emotions ran high during the debate."
  • aim high: to have ambitious goals. "She always aimed high."
  • ride high: to be very successful or in a favorable situation. "The company was riding high after a record year."
  • hold someone in high esteem / regard: to respect and admire someone greatly.
  • be high on something (informal): either to be intoxicated by it, or to be very enthusiastic about it. "The whole team is high on the new strategy."
  • come at a high price: to require great sacrifice or cost, not just money. "Success came at a high price."
Summary of All Meanings

To bring everything together:

Physical: Far above the ground or a base level. (a high shelf, a high mountain, high altitude)

Measurable quantities: Well above the normal or average level. (high temperature, high price, high speed, high quality)

Intensity: Strong, great, or extreme in degree. (high hopes, high praise, high anxiety, high priority)

Rank and importance: Senior or superior in a hierarchy. (high court, high official, high command)

Sophistication: Advanced, complex, or refined. (higher education, high culture, high-tech)

Opinion: Positive and favorable. (a high opinion of someone, hold in high regard)

Sound: Fast-vibrating, sharp, not deep. (a high note, a high-pitched voice)

Peak in time: At the fullest, most intense point. (high noon, high tide, high season, high summer)

Intoxicated: Under the influence of substances, feeling mentally elevated or euphoric. (high on drugs)

Arrogant: High and mighty — behaving as though superior to others.

Joyful: In high spirits — full of happiness and energy.

Strong-smelling (old-fashioned): Food that is strongly scented from aging or slight decomposition.

The single thread connecting all of these meanings is this: high always points above — above the ground, above average, above normal, above others in rank, or above ordinary reality. Whenever you encounter "high" as an adjective and you are not sure what it means, ask yourself: above what? above which reference point? The answer will almost always reveal the meaning.
